title: Poetry Analysis
description: Understanding how poets use language, structure, and sound to create meaning.

notes.heading: Imagery and Sensory Language
notes.body: Imagery refers to language that creates a mental picture or appeals to the senses — sight, sound, smell, touch, and taste. Poets use imagery to make abstract feelings feel real. For example, "golden daffodils that flutter and dance" creates a visual image. Strong imagery is specific and unexpected. When analysing poetry, ask: what does this image make you see, hear, or feel?

notes.heading: Rhyme and Rhythm
notes.body: Rhyme is when words end with the same sound ("moon/June"). A rhyme scheme is the pattern, labelled with letters (ABAB, AABB). Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables — the "beat" of the poem. Regular rhythm can feel calm; irregular rhythm can feel chaotic. Together, rhyme and rhythm give poetry its musical quality.

notes.heading: Structure and Form
notes.body: Structure includes how a poem is organised into stanzas (groups of lines), line lengths, and fixed forms. A sonnet has 14 lines; a haiku has 3 lines (5-7-5 syllables). Free verse has no fixed rhyme or meter. Line breaks create pauses and emphasis. Enjambment is when a sentence runs on from one line to the next without a pause.

flashcards.definition: Descriptive language that appeals to the senses and creates vivid mental pictures.
flashcards.example: "The crimson sun melted into the horizon."

flashcards.definition: The pattern of rhymes at the end of each line, identified by letters (e.g., ABAB).
flashcards.example: Roses are red (A), violets are blue (B), sugar is sweet (A)... — AAB

flashcards.definition: A group of lines in a poem, similar to a paragraph in prose.
flashcards.example: A four-line stanza is called a quatrain.

flashcards.definition: When a sentence or phrase continues past the end of one line into the next without a pause.
Poetry that does not follow a regular rhyme scheme or metrical pattern.

questions.stem: "The moon hung like a lantern over the sleeping city." This line is an example of:
questions.explanation: The line creates a vivid visual picture — this is imagery.

questions.stem: A poem has line 1 rhyming with line 3, and line 2 with line 4. What rhyme scheme?

choices: A group of lines forming a section
When a sentence runs from one line to the next without a full stop
questions.explanation: Enjambment = the sentence continues over the line break without a pause.

questions.stem: A poem with no set rhyme scheme or regular rhythm is written in:
questions.explanation: Free verse has no fixed rhyme scheme or meter.

questions.stem: Why is it important to comment on a poet's specific word choice?
choices: To show you have read the poem
Because all words in a poem are there by accident
Because word choice reveals the poet's intentions and creates specific effects
questions.explanation: Poets choose words deliberately for sound, meaning, and connotation. Analysing word choice reveals mood and meaning.
